title: Arsène Wenger and Arsenal: 30 years on from appointment that changed English football
body: David Dein's decision to hire the Frenchman ushered in an irreversible era of multiculturalism, giving birth to the Premier League we know today As feedback goes, even a character as relentlessly optimistic as David Dein might have considered the reaction to his bold managerial appointment suboptimal. Thirty years ago, Arsenal were in a state of chaotic flux, having sacked Bruce Rioch, with the interims Stewart Houston and Pat Rice in charge. There had been talk of Johan Cruyff arriving and Dein wanted to fill the information vacuum. Summoning the team, he reassured them a new manager would soon be appointed and that he was a world-class addition. "His name is Arsène Wenger," Dein, the club's vice-chair, beamed. A brief pause ensued before a player's voice called out: "Who the fuck is he?" His exclamation echoed conventional wisdom. "Arsene Who?" famously read The London Evening Standard's billboards prior to Wenger being confirmed as manager on 30 September 1996 . Continue reading...

title: Data shows England made inroads against Spain but they must be more clinical | Andrew Beasley
body: Thomas Tuchel's side had 36 touches in the Spain penalty area at Wembley but were given a lesson in taking chances England dominated Spain to an extent very few teams have in recent years. Sadly for them, not in terms of goals . Nor possession. But ownership of the ball is less important than where on the pitch it occurs. Thomas Tuchel's side had 36 touches in the visitors' penalty area, a ridiculously high total when put in context of Spain's last decade. They allowed just 9.5 touches per 90 minutes at the 2026 World Cup. The combined efforts of Belgium, France and Argentina registered 38 touches in the Spain box in the final three rounds of the tournament. Since available records began (at the start of Euro 2016), the most box touches a side has had against Spain was the 45 Germany had in the quarter-final of Euro 2024. However, that game went to extra time. France had 42 in normal time in the ridiculous Nations League semi-final they lost 5-4 last year, then come England, second best in regular time from a sample of 133 matches. Continue reading...

title: Republic of Ireland put controversy aside to earn impressive win over Israel
body: Football and politics are inseparable in the modern world, no matter how many people wish they were not. But whether the beautiful game can ease the ills of our age is another matter. After a week in which the issue of Irish support for the people of Gaza had turned this fixture into a battle of conscience, the outcome of this underwhelming match ultimately felt inconsequential. In the end the result was indeed a walkover, just not because of a boycott. On Saturday night the question had been whether Heimir Hallgrimsson's side would take to the field in Hungary at all. If they did, would their heads be in the game? It turned out that a week of internal angst had been enough to produce collective resolve among the Irish squad, or at least those selected to play. Strong and assertive from the off, their forwards each scored in the first half to settle the contest, with plenty of symbolic action to assure those back home of their feelings. Continue reading...

title: Tony Pulis says he and Stoke were 'cheated' in 2011 FA Cup final after Manchester City verdict
body: Manchester City won match 1-0 after goal by Yaya Touré Club deny wrongdoing and say 'process is ongoing' Tony Pulis has said his Stoke City team were "cheated" out of the 2011 FA Cup after Manchester City were found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules. Pulis's Stoke lost the 2011 Cup final 1-0 after Yaya Touré's goal. Yet following Friday's news that City are guilty on all but one of the more than 100 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, Pulis feels serious discontent. City are expected to appeal and they deny any wrongdoing. Continue reading...

title: OK, now it's time for the Patriots to panic about Drake Maye
body: The New England quarterback was a revelation in the 2025 regular season. But Sunday's loss was just the latest in a series of crushing lows After the Patriots pulled out a win in Week 2 over the Steelers, despite another uninspiring performance from Drake Maye, Mike Vrabel avoided answering questions about his quarterback. Vrabel joked with a reporter not to "ruin my Sunday" when asked about Maye. And this was after a win . On Sunday, Maye was largely responsible for ruining Vrabel's afternoon in the Patriots' 35-6 loss to Jacksonville, which felt like rock bottom (the Pats hope). Simply put, Maye was atrocious. The 2025 MVP runner-up was 14-of-25 for 199 yards, no touchdowns, two interceptions, three sacks, and a lost fumble. Continue reading...

title: Saracens overcome adversity to battle back and edge Leicester in 12-try thriller
body: Leicester 38-40 Saracens Visitors hold on despite Isiekwe's 20-minute red card At the full-time whistle, Brendan Venter let out a roar of delight. Until then the South African had been on his best behaviour, but after beginning his return to the Saracens hotseat with a nail-biting victory against Leicester, Venter could no longer hold it in. title: James Trafford's England dream burns with No 1 spot finally up for grabs again
body: The Leeds player was surprise starter against Spain but, after his solid display, Jordan Pickford's grip may be loosening James Trafford looks genuinely affronted. The Leeds goalkeeper's reaction borders on incredulity. Was it a season of frustration for him at Manchester City last time out, he is asked? A wasted year? "I won two trophies," he says very simply and very firmly. Defiance is the stock in trade of a goalkeeper and Trafford has a nice line in it, on and off the pitch. Thrust into the England lineup against Spain at Wembley on Saturday for only his third cap, he performed well, particularly during the opening 35 minutes when the world champions threatened to run riot. Trafford made two excellent saves that kept England in contention, laying the groundwork for their surge into a 2-1 half-time lead. They ended up losing 3-2 in the Nations League opener after Harry Kane missed a 54th-minute penalty for 3-1. Continue reading...

title: Meet the new minute 55 England collapse, not the same as the old minute 55 England collapse | Barney Ronay
body: Things started to go wrong against Spain at the same time they did against Argentina, but for very different reasons and with far more cause for optimism You could feel it inside the stadium, one of those moments where the air starts to shift, the birds fly backwards through the sky, and outside on Wembley Way an old man clutches his copy of the England Pathway Blueprint to his chest and cowers up at the moon. Welcome to the witching hour, 55 minutes in, when things just seem to happen to Thomas Tuchel's England. Before this Nations League opener there was general agreement on the desirability of systems, pattern, repeatability. And you can't say England aren't consistent. Their last two significant matches, here and in Atlanta in July , have both involved going a goal ahead against the World Cup finalists, playing well and dominating parts of the game, right up until the 55-minute mark. title: Newcastle find themselves the NRL's fairytale team after scarcely believable return to glory | Nick Tedeschi
body: The Knights' incredible preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers showcased everything Justin Holbrook has done to turn the club around Few teams have been mired in mediocrity longer than the Newcastle Knights, a club from a region that few dispute is the heartland of rugby league in Australia. They are built on the legend of Andrew "Joey" Johns and Paul "Chief" Harragon and so many others but have, for the better part of the last quarter-century, been an irrelevance. No more. After one of the most compelling, controversial and climactic preliminary finals in the history of the game, the Knights are on their way to the 2026 NRL grand final just 12 months after claiming their fourth wooden spoon in 11 seasons. Hollywood's finest scriptwriter could not have written the story of Newcastle's rise over the last year – and even the most creative could not have put together what will live in folklore as one of the most dramatic grand final qualifiers the game has seen. title: Brisbane's AFL dynasty is built on sheer talent, a loyal coach and their love of a dire situation | Jonathan Horn
body: Chris Fagan kept faith in his Lions which meant they could thrive with the weight of the football world upon them – and rip out Fremantle hearts There is no precedent for what happened at the MCG on Saturday. There have been devastating finals losses before – the Bulldogs losing the 1997 preliminary final to Adelaide and St Kilda losing the 2009 grand final to Geelong immediately spring to mind. A senior St Kilda staffer described the rooms after that game as resembling "a casualty ward following a mass disaster". Thankfully, we don't talk about sport like that any more. The modern athlete and the modern sporting club is better able to put their world into some sort of perspective. The prevailing mood in the rooms, in the stands and on the trains on Saturday was a mix of desolation and bewilderment. Part of it was Fremantle's history. Part of it was the decision to activate Wharfie Time. Part of it was just how quickly it all happened. You establish an identity and for more than three decades you scratch, claw and hope. And in five minutes, your heart is ripped out. Continue reading...

title: Gateshead's fruitless trip south offers hint of Manchester City's doomsday future
body: His team bottom of the National League, Lee Cattermole's 'bomb squad' approach could well end with him departing Among many doomsday scenarios facing Manchester City is plunging down the football pyramid. Would that be so bad? Instead of yawning at the prospect of yet another meeting with Real Madrid or repeated Avanti train-hampered journeys to Wembley, how about the exoticism of away travel to Wealdstone? In the National League, City's ownership may wish to know, there are no formal financial fair play or strict salary cap regulations. Wrexham, Notts County and Chesterfield have taken advantage of such lax constraints to regenerate. For City fans, Ruislip's buzzy high street, full of nail bars, estate agents and a couple of homely pubs, would represent a welcome world away from Milan's Via Monte Napoleone, as would the suburbia of Grosvenor Vale, Wealdstone's home in the middle of a housing estate, which may jog memories of late-90s visits to Macclesfield and Lincoln. Simpler, happier times, perhaps. Continue reading...

title: ICE has abducted a college athlete. What are the NCAA and universities going to do about it?
body: Aminata Seck's detention shows the bargain facing international college athletes: universities eagerly recruit them, but support can disappear when their immigration status becomes precarious Earlier this week, news broke for the first time that Senegalese Division II Kentucky State women's basketball player Aminata Seck was abducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport on 7 August during a trip to attend the HBCU All-Star game in New York. Seck is listed as a Kentucky State senior and last year started 20 of 26 games, earning third-team all-conference honors and an SIAC Elite 16 award for academic achievement. According to a lawyer involved with her case, Sadiqa Reynolds, Seck has been moved through four different ICE facilities since her initial apprehension: Clay County, Chicago, Clark County and Grayson County. Reynolds noted that the reason for Seck's imprisonment was a missed student visa deadline – what she characterized as "a paperwork situation" – due to back surgery. Reynolds also said that Seck has been suffering from an ACL injury while detained and has received only ibuprofen but no proper medical care. ICE arrests in Kentucky have risen by 70% this year. Nathan Kalman-Lamb is Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of New Brunswick and co-host of The End of Sport podcast. Simran Kaur Sethi is Assistant Professor of Sport Leadership at the University of Kentucky where she studies equity and inclusion for international college athletes. Derek Silva is Professor of Sociology and Criminology at King's University College at Western University and co-host of The End of Sport podcast. Continue reading...

title: The age of asterisk: Manchester City's glittering era of success is tainted now | Barney Ronay
body: Friday's verdict against Manchester City will change everything we understood about their Premier League title triumphs Welcome, then, to the age of asterisk. Whatever punishment Manchester City and their owners receive at the end of this process, the fact remains, everything is tainted now. Overturn the tables, scatter the gold coins. Throw your medals in the bin. You cheated to win them. Whatever that thing was, it's done. Stolen glory, stolen income, stolen joy. Every chant, every "we won the lot", every awkward documentary scene about the deep, throbbing heart of this empire of love. It all looks odd, sinister, cold, sloppy, but also, and this is always the best response, utterly absurd. Continue reading...

title: Messi's exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Jonathan Wilson
body: When things are going awry, the Albiceleste will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause It isn't quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known. Messi's international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn't quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn't care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public's frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game. title: Burnham's booze ruse is a non-starter: just keep doing your drinking in the pub | Barney Ronay
body: The prime minister, a life-long football fan, was just restating a personal opinion about having a drink in the stands, not trying to make policy Hi, I'm Andy Burnham and I don't believe any child should eat gravel for breakfast. title: Mark Wood was a high-speed hero who put body and soul on the line for England | Taha Hashim
body: Fast bowler won the Ashes and two World Cups but those successes were punctuated by long spells out with injury To reach for the career stats on Cricinfo is no way to go about it. This is a full-on YouTube job: boil the kettle, load up those spells at Headingley, St Lucia and the rest, and take in the whippy, absurd, mesmerising sight of perhaps the fastest English bowler there has ever been. That's probably the best way to remember Mark Wood's career. Tuesday's announcement of his international retirement was coming from the moment Wood hobbled out of the Ashes last December, the series opener his only appearance. That always felt like the last act, one he rushed back for after surgery on his left knee earlier that year, and the game moves on fast. England's seam stocks look healthy across formats, with Jofra Archer there to ramp it up when required. It's a sore point that Archer and Wood played just two Tests together: one without supporters during the 2020 Covid-bubble summer, the other Wood's farewell at Perth. Continue reading...

title: 'Hardships never last': Jenn Lichter's path from Colombian orphanage to ultrarunning records
body: Jenn Lichter's childhood followed a difficult path. The resilience she gained helped her achieve an unbreakable ultrarunning feat this summer On 27 June, Jenn Lichter lined up for her first 100-mile race, the Western States 100. The oldest and most prestigious 100-miler in the world, Western States attracts a highly competitive field from around the globe – the athletes run across the Sierra Nevada from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California. Despite 18,000ft of climbing and daytime temperatures often flirting with triple digits, Lichter went in confident. "I wanted to win, there was no secret to that," she says. "That's just who I am." The race remained close for the first half, until the 30-year-old made a move on the climb to Devil's Thumb. The gap grew and at the final aid station, Lichter had a sizable lead over the athlete in second place. A mile from the finish, Nick Cornell, Lichter's fiance, told her she was just ahead of the course record. "That was the first I had heard about it," Lichter says. "He knew my competitive side would jump at the challenge." Continue reading...

title: Sydney Sweeney's cartoonish provocation has sparked a culture war but let's just admit sport can be sexy | Emma John
body: Yes sport is about effort, sweat and inclusivity – but it also turns elite athletes into magnificent specimens of humanity where the aesthetic is part of the appeal Have you seen the 40-second video that will change the way you think about women's sport, women's bodies, just, you know, women? It's been unavoidable on social media this week – brazen, unapologetic, dominating the algorithm like an AI kitten hacking a banana-bread recipe while lip-syncing to Cardi B. I for one have enjoyed it at least 50 times already. It starts with some carefully curated passive-aggression – "Dear Sydney", "Hey Sydney", "Respectfully Sydney" – and follows up with clips of what, in its own words, "a woman in sport actually looks like". It shows its subject pounding the treadmill or powering down the back straight, flooring a rival with a tackle or a roundhouse kick, lifting weights or throwing herself through the air. It is, inevitably, soundtracked by Dua Lipa. Training Season is getting a serious bump this week. Continue reading...

title: Football Daily | Pints and points: the arguments for and against booze at football matches
body: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Considering he is a lifelong Everton fan, it's no surprise that Andy Burnham seems to be in favour of allowing fans to drink Tin at football matches . Bouts of boardroom turmoil, points deductions and assorted relegation battles mean the lot of an Evertonian is not always a happy one. The Prime Minister believes that if he and other fans fancy a sip or two to help ease the pain of watching Thierno Barry head wide of an open goal, then that ought to be their constitutional right as proud Englishmen. Sadly, no such right currently exists, as alcohol consumption within view of the pitch has been outlawed in the top five divisions of English football since the troubled times of the 1980s . Instead, thirsty match-goers are forced to endure an agonising wait of 45 whole minutes before rushing to the bar, joining long queues of fellow fans eager to buy pints of foaming shaft they must subsequently chug back, yard-of-ale style, in enough time to return to their seats for the start of the second half. title: Which football stadiums have the highest and lowest Google ratings? | The Knowledge
body: Plus: the longest waits for 0-0 draws, more early replica kits and champions with the smallest ground Mail us with your all of your questions and answers "As someone who occasionally has to search for stadiums to find directions and the like, I always enjoy that people take the time to rate their experience of visiting a football ground," begins our very own Will Unwin. Pete Tomlin comes up clutch with this answer and one of the most impressive tables in Knowledge history. "I have literally searched every home football ground in the Football League via Google and I have recorded the rating and number of votes for every one," he starts. "The range is not particularly large – the highest recorded rating is 4.7 and the lowest is 4.0. body: Adapting H.P. Lovecraft 's works for the screen in any capacity is not an easy feat. The terrors in the horror author's works are so ambiguous and inexplicable that they rarely translate well to the big and small screens. Despite these challenges, though, some filmmakers have managed to defy expectations and deliver compelling Lovecraftian adaptations. One of these filmmakers is Ridley Scott.

title: The 5 Greatest 5-Season HBO Shows of All Time, Ranked
body: A great show should look different by Season 5. After all, the premise that hooked viewers in Season 1 can't keep doing the work forever. There are only so many times before familiar conflicts start repeating themselves and characters begin running in circles. The best writers understand that reaching Season 5 should mean something has changed along the way. That can be in the form of character growth, changing relationships, and sometimes, even reworking the central conflict of the story.

title: Netflix Is Officially Losing the Biggest Sci-Fi Franchise of the 2010s
body: Netflix hasn't become the biggest streaming service in the world by sticking to only one genre, or even one medium for that matter. Netflix has continued to build on the biggest streaming audience in history by releasing new original projects in various genres, and doing so at such a fast pace that fans are never left without something to watch. Netflix also excels at taking older shows and giving them new life, just like it's done this year with The Last Ship , the five-season sci-fi series led by Eric Dane and produced by Michael Bay . Netflix also found success with the new original sci-fi movie, War Machine , starring Alan Ritchson from Prime Video 's Reacher . After earning a spot in the all-time top 10, a sequel to the film is officially on the way.

title: 'Doctor Who's Legendary Theme Is Part of a 63-Year Old Controversy
body: An outlandish beat, a disquieting whistle, the sound of the TARDIS popping in and out of existence lingering in the back… The Doctor Who theme is by far one of the most unique tunes in the history of television. Originally composed by Australian musician Ron Grainer (and Delia Derbyshire , but we'll get to that), the theme remains pretty much the same since the classic BBC sci-fi series aired its first episode in 1963, with some alterations made by later composers working on the show. This unique theme song has its own wild history behind it. In an era in which now run-of-the-mill synthesizers were still far from becoming a thing, the song was put together through the use of hands-on techniques, from recording jugs of water being poured to simply pressing play on multiple tapes at the same time in order to turn them into a cohesive piece. The result was a distinctive tune that basically introduced the world to the possibilities of electronic music. Add to that a whole in-house debate about who the actual composers of the theme are, and you have yourself a story that deserves to be told.

title: This 100-Year-Old Stunt Spectacle Is Officially Finding New Life on Free Streaming
body: A classic comedy film that turned 100 years old this year is streaming for free on a new platform. Such is the classic film's legacy that not only did it inspire some of the slapstick humor in one 2026 film, but also another — the film's influence could be felt in movies as recent as Zach Cregger 's critically lauded Resident Evil reboot and Minions & Monsters . It's widely considered one of the greatest films ever made, but at the time of its release, it was only a modest box-office hit. Its apparent underperformance caused troubles for its legendary filmmaker, and following the film's release and mediocre performance, his creative freedom was significantly curtailed.

title: Just Play Dead review – Samuel L Jackson and Eva Green punch up switchback crime caper
body: Jackson and Green just about manage to distract viewers from the sub-par Tarantinoesque flourishes, confusing plot points and tired stereotypes Having shot five films since 2020, 82-year-old Martin Campbell is a certified member of the post-retirement director's club that includes Ridley Scott, Martin Scorsese, Woody Allen et al. Samuel L Jackson (a mere 77) sports his worst hairdo since Jackie Brown – a grey, crimped ponytail with an undercut – in this overworked crime caper, though he is on positively cuddly form by his standards. Interrupting his retirement on a Spanish-speaking Caribbean island with the odd poisoning (seen in the intro), kingpin Jack Wolfe (Jackson) is getting antsy. Afraid the law is close behind him, he hatches a scheme with his philandering wife Nora (Eva Green): help him frame her surfer lover Chad (Jason Fernández) for his supposed murder, and they will split the big-bucks insurance payout. He covers his back for the possibility she might do him in for real by recording her saying as much. But she ropes Chad anyway into her murder conspiracy, plotting to let him take the fall – or perhaps her detective bit on the side Dani (Eoin Macken) will get there first. Continue reading...

title: Kikuyu Land review – the colonial-era misery behind our morning cup of tea
body: The impact of colonial then corporate agricultural development is unravelled in a sobering documentary that takes a dramatic turn when a family secret is discovered The central highlands of Kenya are renowned for their lush tea plantations, which stretch as far as the eye can see. Most of the field workers come from the Kikuyu community, whose farming traditions span centuries. In Andrew Harrison Brown and Bea Wangondu's sobering documentary, these resplendent vistas are also enshrouded in misery. Opening with a televised speech by Evelyn Baring, the colonial governor of Kenya during the 1950s , the film lays out the imperialist impetus behind Britain's agricultural development of the country. The Kikuyu people were stripped of their ancestral lands, their labour extracted to enrich their colonisers. This system of inequality continues until now, with multinational corporations taking up the playbook of exploitation left by colonial control. An investigative journalist, Wangondu also appears on screen weaving together a multitude of narratives. There's the decades-long struggle for justice undertaken by Mr Mungai, a pastor and activist who has fought numerous court cases to reclaim his family land. Wangondu talks to plantation workers of past and present, whose harrowing ordeals of physical and sexual violence have been swept under the carpet by both corporate indifference and government corruption. We also hear from an officer in the national intelligence service, who reveals the gruesome methods used by the state to dispose of its critics. These interviews conjure a menacing atmosphere of intimidation and retaliation, from which there seems no way out. Continue reading...

title: Godzilla Minus Zero review – spectacular Japanese action continues franchise's winning streak
body: New York film festival: The follow-up to 2023's Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One dazzles with smart social commentary and jaw-dropping effects Even by the standards of older movie stars catching a major second wind later in their careers, Godzilla pulled off an impressive reclamation of the spotlight three years ago. Godzilla Minus One , the most recent reboot featuring the 70-year-old kaiju – the version(s) from his native Japan, mind, not the Americanized one concurrently starring in a series of Warner Bros blockbusters opposite King Kong – wasn't just another monster-movie success. It fully crossed over, becoming the highest-grossing Japanese-language movie ever released in North America, and won an Academy Award to boot for its terrific visual effects. Now. Japanese Godzilla characters are mainstream enough to pop up in Happy Meals, and the Toho -made sequel Godzilla Minus Zero is world-premiering at the New York film festival. Arguably the artsiest, brainiest of the major fall fests is playing unexpected host to a truly spectacular monster battle royale, packaged alongside some of the same thoughtful historical context that informed the previous film. Writer, director and VFX maestro Takashi Yamazaki returns for the sequel, bringing his lead characters back with him. In the previous film, former military pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki) used his experience with Godzilla to overcome his guilt and shame over failing to complete a pointless kamikaze mission toward the end of the second world war – the devastation of which brought Japan back to "zero", hence a newly emergent Godzilla bringing the country to "minus one". Minus Zero catches up with Kōichi, his now-wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe), and their adopted daughter Akiko (Sae Nagatani) two years later, in 1949 (although Akiko somehow seems more or less the same age). Another monster threat looms over post-war Japan in the form of a dragon-like creature dubbed Ghidorah, whose menace will be familiar to kaiju fans. (Though he isn't seen directly in trailers, this isn't a spoiler; he's featured from the very first scene of the film.) Continue reading...

title: NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary's New York City premiere
body: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel's killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officials The film-makers behind NAZA , the award-winning documentary on Israel's systemic mass killing of Palestinians in Gaza, defended their findings at the film's North American premiere in New York on Saturday, amid protests in Israel and escalating threats from Israeli officials to strip them of their citizenship. The critically acclaimed film , directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, features the testimony of 24 anonymized Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, who describe the AI-powered systems used to select their targets. The project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike , which are often conducted at night in private homes, killing many family members, including children, at once. Continue reading...

title: 'In our deepest hearts we are voyeurs': the paedophile-hunting show that inspired Robert Pattinson's new film
body: Experts and insiders explain how To Catch A Predator became the most controversial show on 2000s TV A man from Long Beach, California, is here to have sex with someone he believes is a 13-year-old girl. When the journalist Chris Hansen walks in, the man's stomach drops. He is caught, and it is the end of his life as he knew it. Hansen asks what his fate should be. "The electric chair?" he asks. No, replies Hansen. "Dateline NBC." This is the opening scene of Primetime , a film directed by Lance Oppenheim, released in the US this week (a UK release follows on 30 October). It explores how a network news show turned sting operations into must-see television, raising a host of ethical questions about justice, voyeurism and society's willingness to dehumanise certain offenders for profit and entertainment. title: Meryl Streep's casting as Aslan has angered the Christian right. Don't they have more pressing issues?
body: The Oscar-winner is voicing Narnia's wise lion in Greta Gerwig's adaptation of The Magician's Nephew, leading to roars of fury from US evangelical commentators It is a confusing time to be alive, given how often these days Hollywood indulges in revisionism. Who knew that the Wicked Witch of the West was the heroine after all, that Cruella de Vil simply had a difficult childhood , or that Mufasa was adopted ? Now it turns out that Aslan, CS Lewis's messiah with a mane, is a lioness – or at least, may sound like one in Greta Gerwig's upcoming adaptation of The Magician's Nephew, because Meryl Streep is providing the voice. News that the Oscar-winner might be portraying Narnia's Christ-like big cat first surfaced in April last year , prompting a flurry of complaints from conservative Christians. This week, the naysayers were back after Empire published a first look at the film , along with an interview with Gerwig in which the director confirmed the casting and explained her choice of actor. Streep, it turns out, was hired not because the Barbie director desperately fancied stoking the flames of controversy, but because she needed someone over 70 who could convey both wisdom and childlike wonder. title: Sense and Sensibility review – Daisy Edgar-Jones leads sober-minded next-gen do-over of Austen romcom
body: With Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as the Dashwood sisters, this fresh take on a beloved classic is not to be confused with Ang Lee's There's no reason for anyone working on a new adaptation of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility to be intimidated by the celebrated 1995 movie by director Ang Lee and screenwriter Emma Thompson, any more than they should be or overawed by Austen's original novel. Sacred cows are there to be … not slain, but re-invented. The decision to bring out a next-gen Sense and Sensibility, with a new young cast – as opposed to, say, a new Northanger Abbey or a new spin on the unfinished The Watsons – might bemuse some and at first it bemused me, like hearing about a Love Actually remake starring Millie Bobby Brown. But this turns out to be a more downbeat, ruminative version, happening in much cloudier weather than 30 years ago and without the sugar-rush final wedding scene. The mood is cooler, but interestingly austere, sober and thoughtful. There are also some strange casting decisions. The sisters at the heart of the story, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, played in 1995 by Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet, are now played by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, and frankly don't look and sound much like the sisters we thought we knew. They look like young women who knew each other reasonably well at uni and are now in a flatshare in London. It is a story of financial and romantic crisis. Mrs Dashwood and her three daughters, having happily occupied a handsome Sussex estate, are forced to move to humble Barton Cottage in Devon when Mrs Dashwood's stepson John Dashwood inherits their property and effectively evicted them. title: Her Private Hell review – Nicolas Winding Refn's shapeshifting fantasia is a dreamy swirl of strangeness
body: Refn's film eludes definition as it moves through time and space, from doomy reality to strange dream worlds populated by quasi-Lynchian characters The title's first word should probably be "His". Nicolas Winding Refn has returned to Cannes with a bizarre new fantasia moodscape, a midnight movie of fear and dreamy disquiet, meaning … what, exactly? The setting of the film – a twist on the 60s pulp shocker of the same title by Norman J Warren – morphs and shapeshifts from place to place, with the antilogical procedure of a dream, from a supposedly real outer world to the inner space of hallucination and memory. It starts in a giant, empty hotel (whose colossal Stygian corridors are not unlike those in Refn's Only God Forgives ) in the middle of a digitally rendered dystopian city, wreathed in the kind of mist that tends to conceal a serial killer, and people here are frightened of someone called the "Leather Man". We move to the fictional action of a movie the hotel's inhabitants are (possibly) planning to make, or perhaps to the world of their fears and imaginings, their ideas occasioned by this ostensible realist premise. And then we move to a situation from the past in US-occupied postwar Japan, where a haunted GI is looking for his daughter. This is a story populated by quasi-Lynchian characters and gargoyles with strange nicknames – the whole imagined landscape, lit by Refn's throbbingly neon purples, reds and blues, looks like a nightclub in hell. And yet it is less violent and explicit than his earlier adventures. The pace is doomy, sepulchral and slow; like Refn's TV series Too Old to Die Young , it moves at the pace of a zombie which has been shot but still keeps on shuffling forward. Or perhaps it is more like that of a sleepwalker who walks and talks slowly, but has a clearer idea of what is happening than those who are, in a more banal sense, awake. Continue reading...

title: Hope review – non-stop gonzo alien battling is top-quality entertainment
body: Na Hong-jin's melee of running, chasing and shouting at the angry invaders is uproarious fun, mixing digital work with old-school spectacle Some uproarious rock'n'roll moviemaking from Korean director Na Hong-jin, a sci-fi action thriller mixing digital work with old-school analogue entertainment values, serving up a spectacle with cheeky touches of Spielberg, Walter Hill and one other director and movie franchise that it would be unsporting to specify at this stage. We are in the remote and sleepy retirees' town of Hope in South Korea near the demilitarised zone (DMZ), where people already constitutionally used to the possibility of war and bloodshed, are astonished to hear of a farm animal killed and mangled – though not for food – by an unidentified beast. title: Boorman and the Devil review – enjoyable re-evaluation of the disaster that was Exorcist II: The Heretic
body: John Boorman generously details the mortifying experience of making a sequel to 1973 hit horror The Exorcist, which was widely and unfairly panned David Kittredge gives us a thoroughly enjoyable, detailed account of the catastrophe that was John Boorman's 1977 film Exorcist II: The Heretic, the deeply ill-conceived and widely derided follow-up to The Exorcist, a bizarre but ambitious fantasy supernatural rhapsody, brimming with unintentional comedy. Yet it was visually bold and even brilliant, pioneering in its use of Steadicam; Linda Blair and Max von Sydow were persuaded to return; Richard Burton was cast as a troubled priest, and Louise Fletcher as a psychiatrist whose weird "mind-reader" contraption was entirely ridiculous. At the first film, people screamed. Now they screamed with laughter. According to an apocryphal tale gleefully repeated by William Friedkin, director of the first film, the sequel resulted in an enraged audience one night turning round and booing Warner Brothers executives in the back row of the cinema, and then chasing them out of the building and down the street. Boorman desperately recut the film with the sillier bits removed. But the damage was done. Continue reading...

title: Remake review – Ross McElwee's magnificent and moving tribute to a tragic loss and the art it inspired
body: Sherman's March director McElwee revisits footage of his late son for this magnificently affecting film and meditation on making art This new film from revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee is an extraordinary work, arguably his most audacious use yet of autobiographical material while at the same time being a coruscating self-criticism of that same technique. Think of it as an artistic ouroboros (a snake eating its own tail). Remake is all at once about creativity, shame, love and loss, revelling in the way film can capture a moment of truth and honesty, but tempered by the knowledge that once a subject knows they're being filmed everything becomes a kind of performance. It's a film that works on so many levels and at the same time is so simple and direct. On that very simplest level, Remake starts out as a documentation of how Hollywood got in touch with McElwee and told him they wanted to make a fictionalised remake of his best-known film, Sherman's March . Made in 1985 with a one-man crew (McElwee himself), Sherman's March recorded the McElwee's trip back to South Carolina where he grew up; there he films his family, old friends, and himself as he continually fails to establish romantic relationships with various women, all of it lavishly slathered with his own warm, softly southern-accented voiceover. title: Manhunter review – Michael Mann serves up a bold and queasy starter to the serial killer spectacle
body: Before Anthony Hopkins' Dr Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, Brian Cox played a cannibalistic killer in Mann's pioneering Red Dragon adaptation Five years before The Silence of the Lambs, there was writer-director Michael Mann's pioneering Thomas Harris adaptation Manhunter, now on re-release in a director's "final cut" for its 40th anniversary. It was his version of Harris's 1981 novel Red Dragon, a movie which features Dr Hannibal Lecter (here spelt Lecktor) in a relatively minor part, and played in a much more coolly matter-of-fact and downbeat way by Brian Cox, who is first discovered in his cell lying down with his back to the camera. It has long been a haughty, hipster film-bro affectation to claim that Cox is better in the role than Anthony Hopkins. (Lecktor's early acoustic stuff was great, you see, before he went electric as Lecter.) I think that's a bit obtuse, for all that Cox is of course very good. Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs is the definitive version: face it. But I will concede that Cox is more interesting than Hopkins by the time the latter came to make the 2002 adaptation of Red Dragon, at which stage the franchise had become a bit tired. Manhunter itself is a very interesting and watchable movie, but feels a little unevolved compared to Jonathan Demme's masterly guignol spectacle, although Demme clearly inhaled Mann's excitement at jets, 'copters and military hardware deployed at speed to bring down just one man. Continue reading...

title: North Sea, Nature Untamed review – stunning footage finds the beauty and splendour under the water
body: Diver Peter van Rodijnen's footage of basking whales, plankton blooms and fatherly fish disputes the idea that the North Sea is a bleak wilderness The North Sea, with its cold grey waters, is the world's drabbest. Or so you might have thought, but this documentary featuring the Dutch diver and underwater cinematographer Peter van Rodijnen sets out to tackle the misconceptions. His stunning footage puts all the splendours of this stormy stretch of water on show, and his voiceover gives it an endearing eccentric charm. First, the greyness. Van Rodijnen films the North Sea's waves sparkling with the cosmic blue light of bioluminescent algae, and lit up with the disco colours of coral and plankton blooms. He also brings us cute, coo-worthy stories from the depths; take the male shorthorn sculpin fish (no looker, it must be said) who spends the winter looking after his eggs, cleaning and blowing fresh water over them. Van Rodijnen's camera is there for the baby fish hatching – pop, pop, pop out of their pearly plump pink eggs. There are some quirky stories, too, including a barnacle with a superlong penis. Continue reading...

title: The Love Hypothesis review – hit BookTok romcom lacks spark on screen
body: Riverdale's Lili Reinhart does some heavy lifting in adaptation of Ali Hazelwood's hit book, but it's not quite enough Fans of the dearly departed Riverdale – or, moreover, admirers of all the batshit things the CW comic soap could make its bright young actors say with straining sincerity – have long rooted for Lili Reinhart. The Betty Cooper of yore was the best of that talented crop (Charles Melton and Camila Mendes among them) at rising above her subpar surroundings, her impressively expressive eyes able to sell the unsellable with complete conviction. She is the type of helplessly endearing performer suited to roles of naivety who masks surprise steeliness, as in her notable turn in 2019's Hustlers or, better yet, romcoms, though there remains a dearth of worthy material. (A dual role in 2022's Look Both Ways , a Netflix homage to Sliding Doors, didn't cut it.) At least on paper, The Love Hypothesis, a new romcom from Amazon Prime Video, should be that material. The BookTok sensation by neuroscientist turned author Ali Hazelwood presents an ideal Reinhart protagonist: extremely nerdy, in a periodic table way, yet conventionally beautiful, awkward and self-deprecating yet cutting when it counts, the type of sweet-presenting young woman who will shout "fuck" repeatedly in private. Which Reinhart's Olive Smith, a young biology PhD student at Stanford, winsomely does in the film's unsettlingly cold open, as a bleary-eyed Olive, blind from expired contacts, freaking out before her grad school interview and then boldly stating her cancer-solving intentions to a brusque, handsome professor in a lab bathroom. Continue reading...

title: Heart of the Beast review – Brad Pitt survivalist dogmance serves up wilderness with side of cheese
body: Pitt and loyal hound Odin get stuck in remote Alaska in this serviceable adventure with hints of Jack London and Marley & Me One man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It's an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy. Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed. Continue reading...

title: Heresy review – feminist folk horror summons something scary in the woods with supply of fresh blood
body: A childless woman flees into the forest and emerges with a swollen belly in director Didier Konings' short, sharp fable Before fertility tourism, the only option for your average medieval serf struggling to conceive was heading to the nearest foreboding woods and summoning weird, antlered dryads. Or so it seems from Didier Konings' short but memorable folk-horror debut, in which wide-eyed villager Frieda (Anneke Sluiters) flees into the trees after escaping an attempted rape by local butcher Gelo (Léon van Waas). He has already told her, after scoffing a pig foetus, that he likes his meat weak and defenceless. The dryads beat IVF hands down. Previously chided for her lack of childbearing by husband Hikko (Len Leo Vincent), Frieda emerges with a swollen abdomen. But the villagers fear it is the devil's work, especially after finding Gelo in the woods, dismembered but freakishly still conscious. That's about the extent of the story here, but Konings pares the focus effectively down to the essentials of this obscurantist hole: the crawling fear of evil among the villagers, and the necessary projection of it on to everything outside their control – female bodies and emotions, the natural world. Though her character verges on symbolic, Frieda – as well as the "wise women" of the forest, as per the original Dutch title – allow this fable's feminist credentials to howl out unmistakably. Continue reading...

title: 'Cracking auction, Gromit!' Original Aardman puppets go under the hammer

title: Global release announced for acclaimed Gaza documentary NAZA
body: Theatrical rollout across 56 territories planned for documentary about Israel's mass killing of civilians in Gaza before film will stream on Guardian website NAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is set to be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries before a digital global release on theguardian.com. The film, which the Guardian produced, premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize . Continue reading...

title: Brigitte Bardot's personal items sell for nearly €1m at auction in Paris
body: Dog collars, guitars and self-portraits among 285 objects, with money going to her animal welfare foundation and son An auction of the French film star turned animal rights activist Brigitte Bardot's personal items has fetched nearly €1m (£858,000, US$1.15m, A$1.61m) in Paris, almost 20 times the estimate, according to the auction house Millon. title: La Bola Negra wins Toronto film festival people's choice award
body: The queer period drama wins Oscar-predicting award, being named the most popular audience film at the festival The Spanish queer drama La Bola Negra has won this year's people's choice award at the Toronto film festival . The film, which takes place in 1932, 1937 and 2017, focuses on the lives of interconnected gay men. It premiered at this year's Cannes film festival with the Guardian's Peter Bradshaw calling it "handsomely produced, lovingly detailed and confidently constructed" in a four-star review. title: 'I get lost going to the bathroom': John Hannah on world travel, stealing props and being 'the Scottish Eminem'
body: The Four Weddings and a Funeral actor answers your questions on being confused with James Nesbitt, his own Sliding Doors moment and a new perspective since turning 60 How often do you get asked to recite that WH Auden poem from Four Weddings and a Funeral , and can you do it from memory right now? mattyjj and simoit Not for a long time. I could probably do the first couple of lines: Stop all the clocks, cut off the telephone / Prevent the dog from barking with a juicy bone / Turn out the lights? And with muffled drums / Something, something … let the mourners come. There you go. Terrible! In Steve Coogan 's Paul Calf's Video Diary, your character praises Orson Welles' The Trial for its "tremendous energy", while Paul says he would "rather watch Dave Lee Travis playing Macbeth". What's your actual opinion of The Trial [by Franz Kafka]? AdrianH1 God, it's a long time since I've read that. I read a lot of those books in my younger days, but probably, like a lot of people, even those who are graduates of English literature, I'd be hard pushed these days to tell you what it was about, other than the persecution of some minor character. title: 'Resident Evil movies? I've never seen one': Weapons director Zach Cregger on resurrecting the beloved zombie franchise
body: Raised on punk, alt-comedy and the church, Cregger's Lynchian approach to horror is anything but typical. After two wildly original hits, his pivot to a 30-year-old video game has caused a storm among protective fans When Barbarian , Zach Cregger's debut film as a solo writer-director, came out in 2022, it was a big success, creating a buzz among horror connoisseurs, garnering good reviews, and grossing $46m. Then his second film, Weapons , came out in 2025 and did even better. Mounting industry buzz around the project crystallised into a fierce bidding war; Jordan Peele was reportedly desperate to produce and, incensed by his failure to secure the rights, allegedly fired his managers. The rumours went viral, resulting in a wave of incredible PR that saw the film wildly outperform box office expectations and win an Academy Award (for Amy Madigan 's blunt-fringed, bonsai-pruning best supporting actress turn as instantly classic villain Aunt Gladys). Even if Cregger had not had a box-office smash that crossed over into awards contention, there would still be an atmosphere of hushed expectation around his next move. Both Barbarian and Weapons addressed hot-button issues – sexual assault and school shootings, respectively – while resisting easy interpretation. Both, too, started out seemingly heading in one narrative direction, before thrillingly careening off elsewhere. Thus, with just two features, Cregger had established a reputation for totally terrifying, utterly unpredictable and – most importantly – genuinely original movies. Continue reading...

title: John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: 'There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way'
body: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete As mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has frequently demonstrated impressive media savvy, but arguably nothing has proved his genius for in-the-know promo more than a video , released in April, with the documentarian John Wilson . The spot, in support of the mayor's plan to reduce the presence of the city's ubiquitous sidewalk sheds, suggested that either he or someone on his team was a fan of How To With John Wilson, the film-maker's cult-beloved HBO series that remains a taste signifier for alt-humorous New Yorkers. And for good reason: over three near-perfect seasons, Wilson, armed with his ever-present camera and diffident, memoiristic narration, explored the city's disintegrating streets with a singular eye for the weird and unintentionally hilarious, turning the most mundane of NYC preoccupations – public restrooms, parking spots, scaffolding – into profound meditations on the glories, indignities and absurdities of modern life. title: Greek epics, gory obsessions and awkward invites: where does this year's Oscars race stand?
body: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey might be the one to beat but a crop of competitors is starting to materialise Reporting from fall film festivals used to be a more streamlined process – what's good, what's bad, what's being sold, what has Oscars chances – but with each year, the season arrives with larger, more existential questions. The 2025 run, from Venice to Telluride to Toronto, was notably underwhelming and took place months after Sinners went from box-office hit to legitimate contender and at the same time as One Battle After Another skipped festivals and went on to win best picture . The pipeline that had once birthed winners such as Birdman, Spotlight, 12 Years a Slave and The King's Speech had no longer played as big of a part with Covid-affected Nomadland being the last fall festival film to win the top prize. Even without an awards hat on, there has been a more general lack of buzz, an excitement of something new that much harder to find as more films of considerably lower quality took up underserved space. If the trades are to be believed, a lot of it is down to studios choosing against the risk of bad buzz and potential embarrassment to A-listers because for every The Shape of Water or Poor Things, there's a White Noise or Joker: Folie à Deux. So while this season might see new films starring Tom Cruise, Timothée Chalamet, Anne Hathaway, Christian Bale, Amy Adams, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Ben Affleck and Mikey Madison, none of them are braving a festival premiere. title: 'The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying': how we made cave horror classic The Descent
body: 'The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower' I was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well … caves . At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, "OK, everybody, turn your lights off" and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn't fathom. title: In an age of superhero fatigue, Marvel's best shot is to think small – and outside the box
body: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light Blink a little and you might think we are back in 2019. The latest Spider-Man film, Brand New Day, has just passed $2.4bn at the global box office, to become the third-highest grossing film of all time behind Avatar and Avengers: Endgame. Meanwhile Avengers: Doomsday is reported to have already earned more than $50m in US ticket presales alone, despite the fact that it doesn't come out until December. Clearly we are in the middle of a superhero renaissance. And yet it doesn't really feel like it, largely because it is something of a turnaround for Marvel, after a pretty disappointing 2025 in which all three of the studio's releases underperformed. Captain America: Brave New World took $415m worldwide, Thunderbolts* managed $382m and even the well-reviewed The Fantastic Four: First Steps stalled at $521m, against a reported $200m budget. These are hardly Madame Web numbers but they do suggest there is still a problem about what to do with all those superheroes who cannot sustain a $300m multiversal extravaganza. Continue reading...

title: Film producer Jeremy Thomas was a cross between a kindly Cambridge don and the movie world's cool uncle
body: The man behind The Last Emperor had the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss along with the soul of a cineaste To say that movie producer Jeremy Thomas was British cinema royalty did not quite do justice to his meritocratic, democratic instincts. A brilliant and inexhaustibly creative man, self-effacingly charming and quietly spoken in a world of loudmouths and show-offs, and hypervigilant for new talent, was more like a cross between an entrepreneur, an enigmatically clever and kindly Cambridge don and the movie world's favourite cool uncle, or maybe cool great-uncle. Respectively son and nephew of directors Ralph Thomas and Gerald Thomas (of Doctor in the House and Carry On fame), he was born into the industry and as an independent producer combined the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss with the soul of a cineaste, backing his own instincts and passions, befriending film-makers and doggedly pursuing projects over years. Continue reading...

title: Gal Gadot's Wonder Woman was one of DC's few successes. It's a mystery why she got the chop
body: James Gunn and Peter Safran's regime had good reasons to ditch Ben Affleck's Batman and Henry Cavill's Superman. Other choices have been much harder to fathom There was never going to be a completely painless way to break up the old DC gang. Warner Bros' DC Extended Universe probably needed to be ruthlessly ripped apart in order to create space for James Gunn and Peter Safran's brand-new DCU. We almost certainly did need a clean break from the likes of Ben Affleck (Batman) and Henry Cavill (Superman), if only to persuade audiences that this really was a proper reboot. The question, as Gal Gadot may have been pondering this week, is quite why some of the old universe's supporting players were smuggled safely into the new continuity while others were left sprawling amid the ruins. Speaking on the Happy Sad Confused podcast , Gadot, who starred in two solo Wonder Woman movies for director Patty Jenkins, revealed that nobody at DC Studios ever formally told her she had been dropped. One minute, Gadot says, she was being assured by Gunn and Safran that they would develop a third instalment with her; the next, she was looking on in mounting alarm as the entire infrastructure of the previous DC continuum was blown to smithereens. "They were like, 'We're going to develop it with you, the third one,'" she said. "But I saw the way everybody else was handled, right? And I, you know – the Henry [Cavill] situation was unfortunate. I was in the middle of that. The Henry situation was not handled elegantly, to say the least. Same with Patty – it was not handled elegantly." Continue reading...

title: Sharvari channels classic Bollywood heroine in Yeh Prem Mol Liya: "It feels incredibly special"
body: Sharvari has shared a graceful dance video on the title track of Yeh Prem Mol Liya , reflecting her love for classic Bollywood music, romance and the traditional Hindi-film heroine. The actor's performance has drawn attention online as she recreates the nostalgic mood associated with the genre. Talking about the video and her connection with Bollywood songs and dance, Sharvari said, "Bollywood songs and dance are actually a big part of why I wanted to become an actor. I grew up watching Madhuri ma'am in ' Didi Tera Devar Deewana ', Karisma ma'am and Sonali ma'am in ' Maiyya Yashoda ', and I would come home and dance to these songs, imagining myself as that heroine on screen one day. I think somewhere, those moments made me fall in love with the idea of Bollywood. "I've always loved the romance, emotion and larger-than-life magic of classic Bollywood songs, the way you could tell an entire story through a song and dance. So getting to experience that with Sooraj Barjatya Ji's Yeh Prem Mol Liya feels incredibly special. It feels like a beautiful full-circle moment, getting to live the kind of Bollywood I grew up watching and dreaming about. I'm genuinely enjoying every moment of it." View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sharvari (@sharvari) Sharvari also shared the video on Instagram with the caption, "Entering my Sooraj Barjatya heroine era with Yeh Prem Mol Liya ." Her post reflects the film's emphasis on romance, innocence and the familiar visual style associated with classic Hindi cinema. The title track features Ayushmann Khurrana and Sharvari and has been composed by Himesh Reshammiya, with vocals by Shreya Ghoshal and Nihal Tauro. The song brings together elements of romance, music and family celebrations, while drawing from the traditional Hindi-film musical format. The track was launched through a live performance at Mumbai's Royal Opera House, accompanied by a 25-piece orchestra. The launch also highlighted the song's orchestral arrangement and its old-school Bollywood-inspired presentation. With her title-track performance, Sharvari offers a glimpse into the musical and romantic world of Yeh Prem Mol Liya . Her comments also highlight how the classic Hindi-film song-and-dance format influenced her aspirations of becoming an actor. title: Vinod Kapri's Pyre to release in theaters on October 23, 2026
body: National Award-winning filmmaker Vinod Kapri's Pyre is set to release theatrically across India on 23 October 2026. Set against the breathtaking Himalayas, the film tells the story of an ageing couple whose lives revolve around their home, their memories and each other, as they quietly wait for their children, who have moved away in search of better opportunities. Produced by Vinod Kapri, Suresh Joshi and Arindra Rai Chaudhuri under the banners Bhagirathi Films and Mashakbeen Studios, Pyre stars debutants Padam Singh Kapri (80) and Heera Devi (70) in the lead roles. Both are from Uttarakhand and had never faced a camera before making the film. Set in a remote village in the Kumaon Himalayas, Pyre explores the emotional landscape of a couple who have spent a lifetime together, while capturing the changing relationship between parents and children separated by migration. The film's extraordinary authenticity comes from its two lead performers. Padam Singh, who plays Padam Singh, is a retired Army man, while Heera Devi, who plays Tulsi, is a widow, homemaker and former dancer. Their real-life experiences and natural chemistry bring an unmistakable intimacy and emotional truth to their relationship. Speaking about the film, director Vinod Kapri said: " Pyre is ultimately a film about love, between two people who have spent their lives together, and between parents and their children. I wanted to tell this story through two people who had lived that life themselves. Finding Padam Singh ji and Heera Devi ji was extraordinary. Their relationship, silences and emotions brought a truth to the screen that conventional actors could never have recreated." Pyre began its international journey with its World Premiere at the 28th Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, where it won the PÖFF Best Film Audience Award. The film has since travelled to several prestigious international festivals, including the 49th São Paulo International Film Festival, 44th Cambridge Film Festival, 35th Bath Film Festival, 43rd Fajr International Film Festival and 30th International Film Festival of Kerala. The film has won 18 international awards, including 15 Best Film Awards, with Best Film honours across Washington, D.C., Chicago, Canada, Spain, Boston, Stuttgart, London and Birmingham. It has also received Best Director awards in Serbia and Boston, along with major recognitions for Music, Cinematography and Sound. Pyre will be distributed theatrically by Cinépolis, which has previously distributed Hanuman Ansh . Adding another distinctive dimension to the film is its music by acclaimed composer Mychael Danna, known for films including Little Miss Sunshine, Monsoon Wedding, Life of Pi and Moneyball , with lyrics by legendary poet and lyricist Gulzar. Shot entirely in the mountains of Uttarakhand, Pyre combines the grandeur of the Himalayas with an intimate portrait of a changing family landscape. title: Fatima Sana Shaikh praises Salman Khan for taking a stand against trolls: "It leaves a lasting impact"
body: Fatima Sana Shaikh has praised Salman Khan for addressing online trolling and speaking up on issues surrounding body-shaming and age-shaming. The actor, who will appear on the upcoming Bigg Boss 20 Weekend Ka Vaar episode to promote her web series Hunkkaar: The Roar , told Salman that his position as a prominent actor allows his words to have a wider impact. In a promo for Sunday’s episode, Fatima brings up Salman's comments from the previous Weekend Ka Vaar. She tells the host that she wanted to speak about the way he responded to trolls and how his decision to address the issue publicly could influence people. Fatima Sana Shaikh said, "Jiss tarike se aapne trolls ko iss baar muh tod jawab diya hai, it’s a huge thing. Kyunki, aapke position mein koi aisi baat karta hai, koi muddon pe khada hota hai, woh bahut hi bada impact deta hai logon pe." The promo does not reveal Salman's response to Fatima's comments. Her remarks come after the actor-host used the previous Weekend Ka Vaar episode to address the trolling he has faced over his appearance, age and personal life. During the episode, Salman took off his shirt and hat while talking about comments surrounding his appearance, including remarks about his hair and body. He also explained that his hairstyle was part of his look for an upcoming film. The conversation later shifted towards the broader issue of online trolling and the way celebrities are targeted on social media. Salman questioned the practice of making money by insulting others and spoke against body-shaming and age-shaming. He also addressed comments made about women after they have children. Without naming Katrina Kaif, who had recently faced online comments about her postpartum body, Salman said that gaining weight after having a baby is normal and that women can work on losing it when they are ready to return to work. Salman also spoke about the paparazzi culture and objected to women being filmed in inappropriate ways. He mentioned that his niece had faced similar behaviour and urged photographers not to share such videos simply for views. Fatima's comments on the upcoming episode add to the discussion around Salman's recent remarks. The actor's response to her praise will be seen when the episode airs. Bigg Boss airs on Colors TV and streams on JioHotstar. title: The Vvaan Box Office: Sidharth Malhotra starrer records Rs. 31.94 crore opening weekend; here's where it stands among 2026 releases
body: The Vvaan: Force of the Forrest has entered the list of notable theatrical performers of 2026 after collecting a revised Rs. 31.94 crore India net in its opening weekend. The Sidharth Malhotra and Tamannaah Bhatia starrer, which released on September 25, witnessed growth over the three-day period and has particularly benefited from mass centres and non-national chains. Trade analyst Taran Adarsh noted the film’s strong performance in Tier 2 and Tier 3 centres, with single screens also contributing to its opening. At Rs. 31.94 crore, The Vvaan currently sits below the year’s biggest opening-weekend performers, led by Dhurandhar The Revenge with Rs. 443 crore. It also trails Spider-Man: Brand New Day (English) at Rs. 257.60 crore, Border 2 at Rs. 129.89 crore, Toxic at Rs. 116.48 crore, Mirzapur: The Movie at Rs. 90.95 crore, Dhamaal 4 at Rs. 64.35 crore, Welcome To The Jungle at Rs 63.47 crore, The Odyssey at Rs. 56.85 crore and Bhooth Bangla at Rs. 54.50 crore. However, The Vvaan has opened ahead of several other notable releases of the year. Its Rs. 31.94 crore weekend is Rs. 23.16 crore higher than Resident Evil’s Rs. 8.78 crore, Rs. 25.36 crore above Vibe’s Rs. 6.58 crore and Rs. 28.20 crore ahead of Daayra’s Rs. 3.74 crore. The revised figure therefore places The Vvaan among the stronger opening weekends recorded by Hindi films in 2026, although the gap between the film and the year’s major blockbusters remains substantial. The next major indicator will be the Monday hold. With the opening weekend now standing at Rs. 31.94 crore, the film’s weekday trajectory will determine how much further it can climb in the 2026 box-office rankings. title: Bigg Boss 20: Gullu chooses 80% ration and restores Uditi Singh and Kanika Mann's lifelines; everyone except Arishfa Khan and Aasif Khan nominated
body: The latest promo of Bigg Boss 20 gives viewers a glimpse into a major decision involving the house ration as well as the upcoming nomination task. With Kushal Tanwar aka Gullu taking charge as the captain of the house for the second time, Bigg Boss placed another crucial choice in front of him, with his decision affecting both the house’s ration supply and the lifelines of contestants. After becoming captain, Gullu was presented with four options. The first offered 120% ration for the house but came without the possibility of restoring any lost lifelines. The remaining three options offered 80% ration along with the restoration of lifelines for different pairs of contestants. The choices were 120% ration with no Jeevandan, 80% ration with the lifelines of Rhiti Tiwari and Yung DSA restored, 80% ration with the lifelines of Aasif Khan and ScoutOP restored, or 80% ration with the lifelines of Uditi Singh and Kanika Mann restored. Gullu ultimately selected the fourth option. As a result, the housemates will receive 80% ration for the week, while Uditi and Kanika will get their lost lifelines back, giving them another chance to remain in the game. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bollywood Hungama (@realbollywoodhungama) Bigg Boss 20 nomination task puts housemates in pairs The latest promo also introduces a nomination task in which the contestants are required to make decisions about their own and their fellow housemates’ safety. The housemates were divided into pairs, with each pair given 10 minutes to decide who would be safe and who would be nominated. The rules added another layer of pressure as both contestants would face nomination if they failed to reach an agreement within the allotted time. Rhiti Tiwari and Amrapali Dubey were unable to reach a consensus, resulting in both contestants being nominated. Mahhi Vij and Arishfa Khan also faced the decision together. Mahhi chose to nominate herself, allowing Arishfa to remain safe. In another pair, Aasif Khan and ScoutOP were given the same choice. Scout opted to nominate himself, which resulted in Aasif being saved. Aman Gandhi and Kanika Mann could not reach an agreement within the given time, putting both of them in the nomination pool. Qazi Touqeer and Uditi Singh also failed to come to a mutual decision, resulting in both contestants being nominated. The final group involved Yung DSA, Love Gill and Mary Kom. The three contestants could not reach an agreement, leading to all three being nominated. With multiple housemates now facing the possibility of eviction, the nomination task is expected to add another layer of competition inside the Bigg Boss 20 house. Meanwhile, Gullu’s decision has restored a lost lifeline for Uditi and Kanika while reducing the house ration to 80% for the week. title: The Grub Fest: Legacy Edit brings the ultimate Punjabi takeover to New Delhi this October
body: The Grub Fest returns to the capital with The Grub Fest: Legacy Edit, bringing together food, music and culture for a two-day celebration on 3rd and 4th October 2026 at NSIC, New Delhi. Marking 12 years of The Grub Fest, the Legacy Edit puts live music at the heart of the festival with what is shaping up to be the ultimate Punjabi takeover of the Grub Arena — bringing together global Punjabi sounds, a new generation of artists and one of the genre's most iconic voices. Leading Saturday night is Gurinder Gill, returning to Delhi with the catalogue that has made him one of the most recognisable voices in contemporary Punjabi music. From global favourites such as 'Brown Munde' and 'Excuses' to fan favourites from his solo catalogue, Gill's headline set is set to be one of the biggest moments of the weekend. title: The Vvaan Box Office: Sidharth Malhotra scores his third highest opening weekend grosser with Rs. 31.94 cr
body: Sidharth Malhotra has registered a major opening-weekend milestone with The Vvaan: Force of the Forrest. The supernatural thriller has collected Rs. 31.94 crore India net in its opening weekend, making it the actor’s highest opening weekend for a film led solely by him. According to box-office data, Param Sundari previously held the record among Sidharth’s solo-led films with an opening weekend of Rs. 28.48 crore. The Vvaan has now surpassed it by Rs. 3.46 crore, representing a 12.15% increase. The comparison becomes even more notable when The Vvaan is placed alongside Sidharth’s entire filmography. Its Rs. 31.94 crore opening weekend ranks third overall, behind Brothers at Rs. 52.08 crore and Ek Villain at Rs. 50.70 crore. Both were multi-starrer films with ensemble lead casts. The film has therefore also moved ahead of Student Of The Year’s Rs. 30 crore opening weekend, giving Sidharth his first opening weekend above the Rs. 30-crore mark as a principal solo lead. The achievement follows an opening day that was already being reported as Sidharth’s biggest solo opener, with The Vvaan estimated at around Rs. 8 crore on Friday. His previous solo opening-day figures included Param Sundari at Rs. 7.37 crore, Marjaavaan at Rs. 7.03 crore and Yodha at Rs. 4.25 crore. With Rs. 31.94 crore in its first three days, The Vvaan has now given Sidharth one of the strongest theatrical starts of his career. The real test, however, begins on Monday, when the film will need to demonstrate whether the opening-weekend momentum can translate into sustained weekday business. title: EXCLUSIVE: Dhruv Tripathi on feature debut Reporting Live starring Parineeti Chopra, "I wanted to make a thriller that feels grounded and real"
body: Dhruv Tripathi is set to make his feature directorial debut with Reporting Live , an investigative thriller set against the world of journalism. The film stars Parineeti Chopra and Deven Bhojani in the lead roles and is scheduled to premiere on Netflix on October 9, 2026. Co-written and directed by Tripathi, Reporting Live follows an ambitious young reporter and her cameraman as they investigate what initially appears to be a straightforward story. Their reporting eventually leads them into the world of illegal sand mining, putting them in conflict with powerful forces that are determined to prevent the truth from coming out. The film also features Adil Hussain, Amol Palekar and Shekhar Suman as part of its ensemble cast. Set within the journalism landscape, the thriller explores the risks involved in pursuing a story while focusing on characters who find themselves dealing with circumstances beyond their control. For Tripathi, the film marks the culmination of a seven-year journey. He developed and wrote the story with Mihir Jadhav before bringing it to the screen as his first feature film. Speaking about his feature debut, Dhruv Tripathi said, "It feels incredibly special to finally announce Reporting Live . I've lived with this film for seven years, from writing it with Mihir to bringing it to the screen, so seeing it ready to go out into the world is quite surreal. I wanted to make a thriller that feels grounded and real, while never losing sight of the ordinary people at the heart of the story. I've been incredibly fortunate to make it with a wonderful cast and crew who brought so much to the film, and I'm really excited for audiences around the world to experience it on Netflix." Tripathi is a graduate of the London Film School's MA Filmmaking programme. Before moving to feature filmmaking, he wrote and directed short films including 10x10ft and Intezaar . His short films have been screened at international film festivals and have received awards for Best Director and Best Screenplay. With Reporting Live , Tripathi moves from short films to his first feature, continuing his focus on grounded and character-driven stories. The film is written by Mihir Jadhav and Dhruv Tripathi and produced by Partha Kiran Thakur and Joshua Shirsath. Drishyam 3 has the added benefit of higher ticket prices, so in terms of gross collections, its advance would be bigger. Stree 2 opened on Independence Day in 2024 and netted Rs. 50 crore on its opening day, which is the benchmark Drishyam 3 will be targeting. Of course, it could go higher, given the higher ticket-price advantage and the fact that there will be no paid previews burning some demand, as was the case with Stree 2.
